title: Design a Leaderboard
summary: A real-time ranking board for a game or app: players submit scores and read the top-K plus their own rank, updated live. The signature challenge is maintaining rank ordering under a high write rate — a Redis sorted set makes score updates and top-K reads O(log N), while cheaply answering a specific user's exact rank at scale is the genuinely hard part.
keyTakeaways: A Redis sorted set (ZSET) is the core data structure: `ZADD`/`ZINCRBY` to update a score, `ZREVRANK` for a user's rank, `ZREVRANGE` for top-K — all O(log N) or better, keeping ordering always-sorted instead of sorting on read.
A relational 'ORDER BY score' on every read is O(N log N) per query and can't cache well under constant score churn; the ZSET amortizes ordering into each write.

Getting one arbitrary user's exact global rank at massive scale is the expensive operation — `ZREVRANK` is O(log N) on a single node but exact rank across a sharded board requires merging shard ranks.
Shard by score range so each shard owns a contiguous band; a user's global rank = (count in higher-scoring shards) + local rank within its shard.
Time-windowed boards (daily/weekly/all-time) use bucketed keys like `lb:daily:2026-07-10` with TTLs, so windows expire cheaply and are queried independently.
Ties are broken deterministically (e.g. encode timestamp into the score's fractional/low bits, or earlier-achiever wins) so rank is stable and reproducible.
Redis is the fast serving layer but volatile — a durable store (the game DB / an append log) is the source of truth so the ZSET can be rebuilt after failure.

questions.prompt: Scope a real-time game leaderboard. What are the functional requirements and the non-functional targets that shape the design?
points: Functional: submit/update a player's score; read top-K (e.g. top 100); read a specific user's rank and nearby neighbors (the 'players around me' view); support multiple boards (global, per-region, per-mode).
Time windows: daily / weekly / monthly / all-time boards, each queryable independently.
Non-functional: very high write rate (every match end updates a score), low-latency reads for top-K and my-rank (<50ms), read-heavy but write-significant.
Freshness: near-real-time — rank should reflect a score within seconds; brief staleness is acceptable, exact-to-the-millisecond is not required.
Scale: state it — e.g. 100M players, tens of millions active/day, millions of score updates/hour at peak.
Tie-breaking and determinism must be specified up front (equal scores need a stable order).
questions.answer: Functionally: players submit scores, and clients read the top-K, a given user's exact rank, and the neighbors around that user, across multiple boards (global, regional, per-mode) and time windows (daily/weekly/all-time). The system is read-heavy but with a serious write rate since every match end mutates a score, and it needs sub-50ms top-K and my-rank reads with only a few seconds of acceptable staleness. At, say, 100M players and millions of updates an hour, the two hard non-functionals are keeping the board sorted under constant write churn and answering an arbitrary user's exact rank fast — and I'd nail down deterministic tie-breaking early so ranks are stable.

questions.prompt: Do a capacity estimate: from active players and match rate, derive write QPS, read QPS, and the memory footprint of the sorted set.
points: Assume 100M registered, 20M DAU; each plays ~10 matches/day → ~200M score updates/day ≈ ~2.3K writes/sec average, ~5-10× at peak ≈ ~20K writes/sec.
Reads: players check rank/top-K more than they play — say 5 reads per match → ~1B reads/day ≈ ~12K/sec avg, peak ~50-100K/sec (heavily cacheable for top-K).
ZSET memory: each member ≈ key/user-id (~20-40 bytes) + score (8 bytes) + skiplist/dict overhead (~64-100 bytes) ≈ ~100 bytes/entry.
20M active entries × ~100 bytes ≈ ~2 GB per board — fits comfortably in one Redis node's RAM; 100M all-time entries ≈ ~10 GB, approaching a single-node limit → shard.
Top-K reads are trivially cacheable (top 100 changes slowly relative to read volume); my-rank reads are the ones that hit the ZSET hard.
Multiple boards (global + regions + daily/weekly windows) multiply memory, reinforcing sharding + TTL'd window keys.
questions.answer: Take 20M DAU at ~10 matches each: ~200M updates/day, so ~2-3K writes/sec average and maybe 20K at peak. Reads dominate — players check standings more than they play — so on the order of 12K/sec average and up to ~100K at peak, though top-K is highly cacheable. Memory-wise a sorted-set entry is roughly 100 bytes with skiplist overhead, so a 20M-active board is ~2 GB (fine on one node) but a 100M all-time board is ~10 GB and starts pushing single-node limits. That, plus wanting per-region and per-window boards, is what pushes me toward sharding and TTL'd window keys rather than one giant ZSET.

questions.prompt: Define the core API and the Redis operations each endpoint maps to.
points: `POST /score {board, userId, score}` → `ZADD board score userId` (absolute) or `ZINCRBY board delta userId` (cumulative) — choose based on whether scores are set or accumulated.
`GET /leaderboard/{board}/top?k=100` → `ZREVRANGE board 0 k-1 WITHSCORES` (highest first).
`GET /leaderboard/{board}/rank/{userId}` → `ZREVRANK board userId` (0-based rank; +1 for human rank) and `ZSCORE` for the value.
`GET /leaderboard/{board}/around/{userId}?n=5` → `ZREVRANK` to find position, then `ZREVRANGE pos-n pos+n WITHSCORES` for the neighbor window.
Board key encodes window + scope: e.g. `lb:global:daily:2026-07-10`, `lb:us-east:alltime`.
Writes go through a service that also persists to the durable store and applies tie-break encoding before ZADD.
questions.answer: Submitting a score is `ZADD board score userId` when scores are absolute, or `ZINCRBY` when they accumulate; top-K is a single `ZREVRANGE board 0 K-1 WITHSCORES`; a user's rank is `ZREVRANK board userId` (plus `ZSCORE` for the value); and the 'players around me' view is a `ZREVRANK` to locate the position followed by a `ZREVRANGE` of the surrounding window. The board key itself encodes scope and window — `lb:global:daily:2026-07-10` or `lb:us-east:alltime` — and every write flows through a service that also writes the durable store and applies the tie-break encoding before the ZADD.

options: SQL cannot store integers large enough for game scores
The sorted set keeps entries continuously ordered so top-K and rank are O(log N), whereas the SQL query re-sorts up to O(N log N) per read and caches poorly under constant score churn
Redis is durable and SQL is not, so Redis never loses the leaderboard
SQL cannot compute a specific row's rank at all
questions.explain: The sorted set amortizes ordering into each write (an O(log N) skiplist insert), so top-K is an O(log N + K) range read and a user's rank is an O(log N) `ZREVRANK` — always fresh, no re-sort. The SQL approach re-derives the order per query, which is expensive at scale and hard to cache because scores change constantly, invalidating any cached page. SQL can compute rank (via window functions/counts) and is in fact the more durable store — so those options are wrong; the real reason is the sorted-set's always-sorted structure and read complexity.
questions.q: Why use a Redis sorted set instead of storing scores in SQL and running `SELECT ... ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100` on each read?

questions.prompt: The signature deep-dive: getting one arbitrary user's exact global rank is the expensive operation at scale. Why, and how do you shard the board and still answer it?
points: On a single node `ZREVRANK` is O(log N) and cheap — the problem appears once the board is too big for one node and must be sharded.
Exact rank is inherently global: your rank = the count of everyone scoring higher, which spans all shards, so no single shard knows it locally.
Shard by score range (not by user hash): each shard owns a contiguous score band, so higher-scoring shards are fully 'above' a user by definition.
Global rank = sum of `ZCARD` of all strictly-higher shards + local `ZREVRANK` within the user's own shard — a bounded fan-out (number of shards), not a full scan.
Keep per-shard counts/boundaries cached so the 'count higher shards' step is O(#shards); rebalance bands as the score distribution drifts.
If exact rank isn't required, approximate it: histogram/percentile buckets give 'top ~5%' in O(1) and dodge cross-shard fan-out entirely — a common real-world compromise.
questions.answer: On one node `ZREVRANK` is a cheap O(log N), so the pain only starts when the board outgrows a single node and shards. Exact rank is fundamentally global — it's the count of everyone above you — so no single shard can answer it alone. The trick is to shard by score range rather than by user: each shard owns a contiguous band, so a user's global rank is the summed cardinality of all strictly-higher shards plus its local `ZREVRANK` within its own band, which is a fan-out over the number of shards, not a full scan. I cache each shard's boundaries and counts so the 'count above' step is O(#shards), and rebalance bands as the distribution drifts. When exact rank isn't truly needed, I'd switch to percentile buckets — 'you're in the top 3%' — which is O(1) and sidesteps the cross-shard fan-out entirely.

questions.prompt: How do you implement time-windowed boards (daily/weekly/all-time) and handle ties deterministically?
points: Windowed boards = separate keys with the window baked in: `lb:daily:2026-07-10`, `lb:weekly:2026-W28`, `lb:alltime`; a score update writes to all relevant window keys.
Set a TTL on window keys (e.g. daily key expires after 48h) so old windows self-clean; all-time has no TTL and is the one to shard.
Weekly/monthly can be derived by unioning day keys (`ZUNIONSTORE`) instead of double-writing, trading read cost for write simplicity — a real tradeoff to name.
Ties: sorted sets order equal scores lexicographically by member, which is arbitrary/unfair — instead encode the tiebreak into the score.
Common trick: composite score = primary_score in the high bits + inverted timestamp in the low bits (earlier achiever ranks higher on equal score), stored as one 64-bit/float value.
This keeps a single `ZADD` and a single `ZREVRANK` while making ranks deterministic and reproducible across rebuilds.
questions.answer: Each window is just a differently-keyed sorted set — `lb:daily:2026-07-10`, `lb:weekly:2026-W28`, `lb:alltime` — and a score update fans out to the relevant ones. Daily/weekly keys carry a TTL so they self-expire, while all-time is the durable, shard-worthy one; alternatively I can avoid double-writing and derive weekly on read by `ZUNIONSTORE`-ing the day keys, trading read cost for write simplicity. For ties I don't rely on Redis's lexicographic member ordering because it's unfair — I encode a composite score with the real score in the high bits and an inverted timestamp in the low bits, so an earlier achiever wins an equal score. That keeps everything a single `ZADD`/`ZREVRANK` while making ranks deterministic and reproducible if I ever rebuild the board.

options: Hash the user ID to a shard, then query every shard for its local top 100 and merge
Put every write on a single shard and replicate it read-only to the others
Shard by score range so the highest band's shard already holds (most of) the global top-K, minimizing fan-out
Randomly assign each score update to a shard to spread load evenly
questions.explain: Range-sharding by score means the top-K lives in (or starts at) the highest-score shard, so top-100 is answered from essentially one shard instead of scatter-gathering from all of them. Hash-by-user spreads a given score band across every shard, forcing you to query all shards and merge for any top-K or rank query. A single write shard just recreates the single-node bottleneck, and random assignment has the same scatter-gather problem as hashing. Range-sharding aligns the physical layout with the query (ordering), which is the whole point.
questions.q: You shard the leaderboard across nodes to fit memory. To answer 'top 100 globally' efficiently, which sharding scheme is best?

questions.prompt: Redis is in-memory and volatile. How do you make the leaderboard durable and recover it after a Redis node failure?
points: Treat Redis as the fast serving/index layer, not the source of truth: every score write is also persisted to a durable store (game DB row and/or an append-only score-events log).
On Redis loss, rebuild the ZSET by replaying the durable scores — for all-time, from the DB's current-best per user; for windows, from the events log filtered to the window.
Use Redis persistence (AOF/RDB) + replicas for fast failover so you rarely do a full rebuild; replicas also serve reads.
Make writes idempotent (ZADD with absolute score is naturally idempotent; ZINCRBY needs dedupe keys) so replay/retries don't double-count.
Warm caches / accept brief staleness during rebuild; top-K can be served from the DB temporarily.
Cross-region: async-replicate the durable store; regional Redis boards are rebuildable locally, keeping the volatile layer disposable.
questions.answer: I treat Redis as a rebuildable index, not the truth: every score update also lands in a durable store — the game DB's best-score-per-user for all-time, plus an append-only events log for windowed boards. If a node dies I fail over to a replica (Redis AOF/RDB + replication makes this fast), and worst case I rebuild the ZSET by replaying the durable scores. I keep writes idempotent — absolute `ZADD` is naturally idempotent, and cumulative `ZINCRBY` gets a dedupe key — so replays don't double-count, and during a rebuild I can temporarily serve top-K from the DB and accept a few seconds of staleness. Because the durable store is the authority, the whole in-memory layer stays disposable and regionally rebuildable.

questions.prompt: Staff-level: at peak, hot boards get hammered by both writes and my-rank reads. Where does this design strain, and how do you evolve it?
points: Write hotspot: a single mega-board's ZSET is one node's write throughput ceiling — range-shard it and/or batch/coalesce rapid updates for the same user before ZADD.
Read hotspot on top-K: cache the top-K page (it changes slowly) at the edge/app layer with a short TTL, serving the vast majority of reads without touching Redis.
my-rank reads are the un-cacheable tail (unique per user) — this is the load that justifies sharding-by-score and/or serving approximate percentile rank instead of exact.
Consistency tradeoff: accept eventual/near-real-time rank; a few seconds of staleness lets you batch writes and cache reads aggressively.
Abuse/correctness: validate/authenticate score submissions server-side (anti-cheat), rate-limit, and reconcile Redis against the durable store periodically to catch drift.
Global scale: per-region boards with a rolled-up global view (union/merge) avoids one global write bottleneck while still offering a global ranking.
questions.answer: The two strain points are the single-board write ceiling and the un-cacheable my-rank read. I relieve writes by range-sharding the board and coalescing rapid same-user updates before the ZADD, and I relieve top-K reads by caching that slowly-changing page at the app/edge with a short TTL so most reads never hit Redis. The genuinely hard load is per-user exact rank, which is unique per request — that's what justifies score-range sharding, and where I'd offer approximate percentile rank when 'top 3%' is good enough. I lean on near-real-time consistency to enable that batching and caching, add server-side score validation and rate limits for anti-cheat, periodically reconcile Redis against the durable store, and go per-region-with-a-global-rollup so no single node is the global write bottleneck.
